title: Minor burn first aid
summary: A friend grabs a hot beaker. Cool it, take off her ring, cover it, and know when it isn't minor.
sources: Indian Red Cross Society / St John Ambulance first aid: burns

scenes.narration: Your friend grabs a beaker that has just come off the tripod and yelps. Two fingertips are red and stinging.
scenes.prompt: Spot the problem. Pick "Point it out" and tap it.

hints.text: Your friend yelped and is holding her hand. What exactly got hurt?
Pick "Point it out" and use it on her burned fingertips.

choices.label: Point at her fingertips: that's a burn, cool it now
choices.feedback: Yes. A burn keeps cooking the skin after the contact ends. Cooling quickly limits the damage.

choices.label: Check whether the beaker is cracked first
choices.feedback: The beaker can wait. Your friend's fingers can't: every second of cooling counts.

choices.label: Tell her to shake it off, it'll be fine
choices.feedback: Shaking it doesn't cool it. Get it under cool running water straight away.

scenes.narration: The red area is smaller than her palm and the skin isn't broken. She isn't feeling faint.

hints.text: Smaller than her palm, skin not broken, not feeling faint: does that sound like a small burn or a serious one?
Look at your teacher: they need to know about any injury in the lab.
Use your hands on your teacher: it's a minor burn, so tell them and start first aid.

choices.label: Small and unbroken: a minor burn. Tell the teacher and start first aid
choices.feedback: Right. Small, unbroken burns can be treated with first aid. Still tell the teacher.

choices.label: It's severe: call an ambulance
choices.feedback: This one is minor. Call 112 for large or deep burns, burns on the face, hands or feet of a young child, or chemical and electrical burns.

scenes.narration: What first aid do you give?
scenes.prompt: Cool the burn: drag something onto it.

hints.text: Heat keeps damaging skin until it's cooled. What cools it gently, and for how long? (Ice is too harsh.)
Look at the cold tap over the sink.
Use your hands on the cold tap: hold her fingers under cool running water for 20 minutes.

choices.label: Hold her fingers under cool running water for 20 minutes
choices.feedback: Correct. Cool (not icy) running water for 20 minutes is the most important step. It still helps up to 3 hours after a burn.

choices.label: Hold ice on it
choices.feedback: Ice is too cold: it can damage the skin further, like frostbite. Use cool running water instead.

choices.label: Rub butter on it
choices.feedback: Never use butter, ghee or oil: they trap the heat in and can cause infection.

choices.label: Put toothpaste on it
choices.feedback: Toothpaste doesn't cool a burn. It traps heat and can irritate and infect the skin. Water only.

scenes.narration: Her fingers are cooling under the tap. You notice she's wearing a ring on the burned hand.

hints.text: Burned skin swells. What could get stuck on a swollen finger?
Look at the ring on her burned hand.
Use your hands on the ring: slip it off gently before the finger swells.

choices.label: Gently slip the ring off before the finger swells
choices.feedback: Yes. Burned skin swells. Take off rings, watches and bangles near the burn early, unless they're stuck to the skin.

choices.label: It's only a ring, leave it on
choices.feedback: Swelling can trap a ring and cut off blood flow. Remove jewellery near a burn early.

scenes.narration: After 20 minutes the stinging has eased. A small blister is forming on one fingertip.

hints.text: A blister is the body's own clean dressing. What would protect it without sticking to it or leaving fibres?
Lay the cling film loosely over the burn. Don't wrap it tight.

choices.label: Lay cling film loosely over it (don't wrap it tight)
choices.feedback: Yes. Cling film laid loosely keeps the burn clean without sticking. A clean, non-fluffy dressing works too.

choices.label: Pop the blister so it heals faster
choices.feedback: Don't burst blisters: they protect the skin underneath from infection.

choices.label: Wrap it in cotton wool
choices.feedback: Cotton wool fibres stick to burns. Use cling film or a non-fluffy dressing.

scenes.narration: The burn is covered. The blister is about the size of a coin.

hints.text: It has blistered. Should someone trained take a look?
Use your hands on your teacher: tell them it has blistered so the school nurse or a doctor can check it.

choices.label: Tell the teacher it has blistered, so the school nurse or a doctor can check it
choices.feedback: Right. Blistered burns should be checked by a nurse or doctor. Get urgent help (112) if a burn is large, deep, on the face, or the person feels unwell.

choices.label: It's covered now, so get back to the experiment
choices.feedback: A burn that has blistered should be checked by a nurse or doctor. Tell the teacher.

end-safe.text: The burn heals over the next week. Quick cooling made all the difference.

learn: Cool a burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, as soon as possible.
Remove rings, watches or bangles near the burn before it swells.
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing.
No ice, butter, ghee, oil or toothpaste; don't burst blisters.
Get a blistered burn checked. Call 112 for large or deep burns, burns to the face, chemical or electrical burns, or burns on young children.
disclaimer: Training only. This is not a substitute for emergency services or certified first-aid and fire-safety training. In a real emergency in India, call 112.
